strengths: Addresses a well-motivated gap from Zaremba et al. (2025): why inference-time compute defenses fail against gradient-based/multimodal attacks, and proposes a plausible unifying explanation (the RICH hypothesis) tied to compositional generalization.

Reasonably broad set of complementary experiments: explicit vs. implicit security specifications, white-box PGD attacks at varying epsilon, naive prompt-based compute scaling, CoT-based scaling on Attack-Bard, and extension to large open-source VLMs (Qwen-2.5-VL-72B, Llama-3.2-Vision-90B) to rule out scale as a confound.

Provides some statistically-tested results (McNemar's test) for the CoT/Attack-Bard experiments (Tables 3-4), and qualitative/interpretability evidence (attention maps, attack image changes in Figure 1) that is intuitive and illustrative.

Offers actionable, practical guidance (layering lightweight adversarial finetuning with test-time compute) that could be useful for practitioners, and reframes prior negative findings in a constructive way.
Clear writing structure with explicit hypotheses, predictions, and dedicated 'takeaway' boxes after each experiment aiding readability.
weaknesses: Central claims rest on very small sample sizes in key ablations (e.g., Table 1 uses only 2 replicates; Section 4.2/4.3 use only 4 base images across 3 attack variants = 12 conditions), which is weak evidence for the strong causal 'rich-get-richer' narrative being advanced.

The core finding risks being somewhat tautological: models adversarially trained on gradient-based perturbations are, by construction, more robust to similar gradient attacks and better preserve instruction-following, so it is unsurprising that prompting/compute scaling has more headroom to exploit on top of already-robust base representations. The paper does not clearly disentangle 'compositional generalization enabling specification-following' from the simpler explanation that adversarial training directly improves robust perception/representations, independent of any specification-following mechanism.

The RICH hypothesis is qualitative and not made operationally precise (e.g., no explicit distance metric quantifying 'closeness' of attacked data components to training distribution), limiting its falsifiability and predictive precision beyond directionally-consistent trends.

Evidence for the compositional-generalization mechanism itself is largely anecdotal (a single qualitative example in Figure 1's attention maps) rather than a systematic mechanistic analysis (e.g., probing, representation similarity, or ablations isolating instruction-following from perceptual robustness).

Model diversity is narrow: nearly all core experiments use the same LLaVA-v1.5 architecture family with varying degrees of adversarial training, rather than a broader set of independent architectures/robustification methods, limiting generalizability claims.

The large-scale VLM results (Table 4) show no significant CoT benefit even on clean data in one case and no benefit on adversarial data for both large models, which somewhat undercuts the paper's practical relevance since most large-scale/frontier models are not adversarially pretrained and the approach seems to require costly adversarial training to unlock any benefit.

No comparison to alternative or competing defense/compute-scaling baselines (e.g., other prompting strategies, ensembling, or certified defenses), making it hard to judge the practical significance of the proposed synthesis relative to existing alternatives.

Compute-scaling operationalizations (naive prompt repetition K times, CoT with fixed token budgets) are somewhat ad hoc proxies for 'inference compute' and diverge from the RL-tuned extended reasoning studied in the motivating prior work, raising questions about how well conclusions transfer to true RL-based reasoning scaling in frontier models.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated gap in Zaremba et al. (2025): why does test-time compute fail to defend against gradient-based/multimodal attacks, and proposes an interpretable hypothesis (RICH) to explain it.

Uses a useful 'robustness ladder' of publicly available LLaVA variants (LLaVA-v1.5, FARE-LLaVA, Delta2LLaVA) spanning low-to-high adversarial training, which enables a reasonably controlled comparison of how base robustness interacts with inference-compute scaling.

Extends beyond the original black-box setting to include novel protocols: explicit security specifications, white-box PGD attacks, varying attack budgets, and pre-filled responses to isolate confounders.
Reports statistical significance (McNemar's test) for CoT benefit claims and includes some replicate/error-bar reporting.
Includes an interesting qualitative analysis (attention maps, interpretable attacks) that adds some mechanistic color to the quantitative findings.
weaknesses: The central mechanistic claim (compositional generalization unlocks specification-following on OOD data) is never directly measured or ablated; it is inferred post-hoc from correlational outcomes between base model robustness and inference-compute gains, making the explanatory story more narrative than demonstrated.

Severe confound between 'degree of adversarial training' and many other differences between LLaVA, FARE-LLaVA, and Delta2LLaVA (different pretraining data, CLIP variants, instruction-tuning procedures, perturbation budgets used in training). Attributing the entire effect to the amount of attacked-data exposure versus these other differences is not well isolated.

Sample sizes are very small in several key experiments (e.g., Table 1 uses only 2 replicates; Table 2 uses only 4 images across 3 attribute types), undermining confidence in the reported trends, especially given the strong causal claims made from them.

Results on larger-scale, non-adversarially-trained VLMs (Qwen-2.5-VL-72B, Llama-3.2-Vision-90B) in Table 4 show no significant CoT robustness benefit even on clean-performance-matched tasks, which is consistent with but also under-explores the hypothesis at scale; the paper does not test any large-scale robustified model, leaving the central claim about generalization across scale largely untested.

The attack scenarios are fairly narrow/contrived (single-word shape/color/texture classification, a toy visual prompt injection), raising concerns about ecological validity for realistic jailbreak or safety-critical settings.

The hypothesis, as stated, is fairly unsurprising/intuitive (more robust models remain more robust, and additional compute amplifies this), and the paper does not clearly articulate what a falsifying result would look like or compare against simpler alternative explanations (e.g., simply that robustified models have higher baseline accuracy/logit margins, independent of any 'compositional generalization' story).

The experimental narrative shifts across sections (naive prompt repetition scaling, CoT, explicit vs. implicit specifications), which, combined with the exploratory framing in Section 2 feeding into confirmatory claims later, raises concerns about post-hoc rationalization/HARKing rather than a rigorously pre-specified test of a single hypothesis.

Clarity and framing issues: the colloquial title and some stylistic choices may not suit a top-tier technical venue, and the paper's core contribution (robustness compounds with robustness) is incremental relative to established findings about adversarial training and generalization.

strengths: Proposes a clear, falsifiable hypothesis (RICH) that directly addresses an acknowledged gap in Zaremba et al. (2025) — namely why inference-compute defenses fail against gradient-based/multimodal attacks — and offers an intuitive, mechanistically motivated explanation grounded in compositional generalization.

Tests the hypothesis across a reasonably diverse set of conditions: three attack strengths/types (black-box Attack-Bard, white-box PGD visual prompt injection, white-box PGD shape/color/texture classification), multiple models spanning low/medium/high base robustness, and multiple inference-scaling strategies (naive specification repetition, CoT).

Includes thoughtful controls, such as pre-filling model responses to isolate whether specification tokens alone (rather than generalized instruction-following) drive robustness, and varying attack budget ε to test the 'distance to training distribution' prediction directly.

Extends analysis to larger open-source VLMs (Qwen-2.5-VL-72B, Llama-3.2-Vision-90B) to rule out model/data scale as a confound, and uses statistical testing (McNemar's test) to assess significance of CoT benefits.

Provides practically useful takeaways (e.g., lightweight adversarial finetuning can unlock inference-compute's robustness benefits) and interesting qualitative evidence (attention maps, attack interpretability) that support the proposed mechanism beyond aggregate accuracy numbers.
weaknesses: Several key experiments rely on very small samples (e.g., 2 replicates in Table 1, 4 images × 3 attributes in Table 2/Figure 3), raising concerns about statistical power and the reliability of trends, especially since no confidence intervals are shown for many plots (e.g., Figure 3 top).

The core evidence is built around only three LLaVA-family checkpoints that differ in several ways beyond 'degree of adversarial training' (different vision encoders, finetuning data, pipelines), so the causal attribution of robustness differences specifically to compositional generalization from training-data overlap is not fully isolated from other confounds.

The hypothesis itself is somewhat qualitative/hard to falsify — 'training data better reflects attacked data's components' is not operationalized with a concrete, measurable distance metric, making it difficult to assess predictive precision beyond post-hoc narrative fit.

Results on larger-scale VLMs (Table 4) show CoT provides no significant benefit on adversarial data for either Qwen or Llama (even on clean data for Llama), which somewhat complicates the clean 'rich-get-richer' narrative and is explained away rather than directly tested with a controlled adversarial-training manipulation at that scale.

The paper explicitly avoids testing with RL-finetuned reasoning models, which was the actual setting motivating the original gap in Zaremba et al.; this leaves open whether RICH's dynamics hold in the regime that prompted the investigation, somewhat limiting the work's direct relevance to that motivating case.

Evaluation remains largely confined to simple visual classification/description and template-based prompt injection tasks rather than more realistic, diverse jailbreak/harm scenarios, limiting evidence for broader practical significance of the claimed robustness gains.

Presentation is at times informal (e.g., title framing) and the paper would benefit from tighter formalization of the hypothesis and a more systematic ablation isolating 'compositional generalization' from simple correlation with adversarial training strength.

strengths: Addresses a timely and important gap: why inference-time compute defenses (à la Zaremba et al. 2025) fail against gradient-based/multimodal attacks, and what conditions restore their benefit.

Broad experimental scope: multiple model families with varying levels of adversarial training (LLaVA-v1.5, FARE-LLaVA, Delta2LLaVA, InternVL 3.5, Qwen-2.5-VL-72B, Llama-3.2-Vision-90B), multiple attack types (black-box transfer, white-box PGD at varying epsilon), and multiple inference-scaling strategies (naive specification repetition, CoT, budget-forced reasoning).

Thoughtful control experiments that attempt to rule out confounds, e.g., testing random-token prefill/padding vs. specification-consistent content, and varying the attack budget to test the 'distance to training distribution' mechanism.

Provides some qualitative/interpretability evidence (attention maps, reasoning trace content, attack image visualizations) that adds plausibility to the proposed compositional-generalization mechanism beyond pure aggregate metrics.

Practical, actionable takeaway: even lightweight adversarial finetuning of a vision encoder can be enough to unlock the benefits of test-time compute scaling, which is a useful and reasonably well-supported practical recommendation.
weaknesses: The central hypothesis (RICH) is somewhat unsurprising/incremental: that inference-time defenses work better when the base model is already more robust/generalizes better is close to a restatement of known synergy between train-time and test-time robustness, rather than a sharply novel mechanistic claim.

Statistical power is weak in several key experiments: e.g., Table 2 uses only 2 replicates, Tables 3/7/8 use only 3-4 images, undermining confidence in the reported trends, especially given the qualitative/rhetorical framing ('rich-get-richer') applied to fairly small numeric differences (e.g., Figure 1's ~29%→31.5% accuracy shift).

The models compared (LLaVA-v1.5, FARE, Delta2) differ not only in robustness level but in vision encoder, pretraining data, and instruction-tuning pipeline; the paper does not fully rule out that these confounds (rather than 'robustness' per se) drive the observed differences in inference-time-compute benefit.

The mechanistic claim (compositional generalization) is inferred largely qualitatively (attention maps, reasoning trace counts) rather than directly and rigorously measured/quantified, leaving the causal story more asserted than demonstrated.

Results for large-scale models (Qwen-2.5-VL-72B, Llama-3.2-Vision-90B) are mixed/weak and somewhat undercut the 'model scale doesn't explain it' argument (e.g., Llama shows no CoT benefit even on clean data), yet this is not discussed as a limitation in depth.

The paper only studies vision-language models and visual attacks; it does not revisit the original text-jailbreak setting from Zaremba et al. to test whether RICH's predictions hold there too, limiting generality of the claimed hypothesis.

Multiple significance tests (McNemar's) are run across many model/condition combinations without correction for multiple comparisons, and some 'benefit' vs 'no benefit' conclusions rest on borderline p-values.

Dense, rhetorically flourished framing (RICH acronym, 'get rich or die scaling') and heavy reliance on informal narrative ('the rich get richer') somewhat obscures precise quantitative claims and effect sizes.

strengths: Proposes a clear, falsifiable hypothesis (RICH) connecting base-model robustness, compositional generalization, and the effectiveness of inference-time-compute defenses, directly addressing an open question left by Zaremba et al. (2025) regarding why reasoning-based defenses fail against vision/gradient attacks.

Broad experimental sweep: multiple models with varying robustness levels (LLaVA-v1.5, FARE-LLaVA, Delta2LLaVA, InternVL 3.5, Qwen-2.5-VL-72B, Llama-3.2-Vision-90B), multiple attack types (black-box transfer, white-box PGD, prompt injection), and multiple inference-scaling strategies (naive repetition, CoT, budget-forced reasoning).

Useful control experiments (random token pre-fill, random token scaling instead of security-specification text) that help rule out trivial confounders such as 'more tokens = more robustness' and support the specification-following interpretation.

Practical, actionable takeaway: lightweight adversarial finetuning (e.g., FARE-style embedding tuning) can be combined with test-time compute to cheaply unlock robustness gains, which is a reasonably actionable recipe for practitioners.
Appendix material (frontier-model description-then-classify pipeline, additional ablations on attack budget and token content) adds some robustness-checking depth beyond the main text.
weaknesses: The central claim is tested mostly through small-sample, high-variance experiments (e.g., 4 images with 3 attack variants and 2 replicates in Table 3, 2 replicates in Tables 2/6), undermining confidence in the reported 'rich-get-richer' trend; error bars in Figure 4/Table 3 are often very large relative to the effect sizes being claimed.

The large-scale model results (Table 5), which are presented as validating that model/data scale does not explain the findings, actually show weak or no CoT robustness benefit for Llama-3.2-Vision-90B and only marginal/non-significant benefit for Qwen-2.5-VL-72B on adversarial data — this is in tension with the paper's framing of 'broad support for the RICH' and is not critically discussed.

Compositional generalization, the proposed causal mechanism, is never directly measured; it is inferred post hoc from correlations between base robustness and specification-following under attack. Alternative explanations (e.g., general instruction-following capability, reduced perturbation sensitivity from adversarial training, or simple shift in output distribution due to robust training) are not rigorously ruled out.

The experimental protocol for 'scaling inference compute' changes across sections (naive repetition of the specification K times, CoT with a fixed token cap, budget-forced reasoning) without a unified justification, making it unclear whether the observed effects generalize to genuine reasoning-driven test-time compute or are artifacts of the specific scaling heuristic used (e.g., repeating a specification string).
Key qualitative claims (e.g., the weevil example in Figure 1, counting snout mentions 28 vs 4 times) are anecdotal and not substantiated by systematic analysis of reasoning traces across the dataset.

Statistical testing is somewhat inconsistent: significance is assessed via McNemar's test at p<0.01, but borderline cases (e.g., p=4.2e-2 for LLaVA-v1.5 in Table 4) are labeled 'No' while being close to conventional significance, and the overall framework does not correct for multiple comparisons across the many experimental configurations.

The 'first adversarially robust RL-tuned reasoning VLM' contribution claimed in the introduction is not substantively presented or evaluated in the main paper; details are relegated to a brief appendix section with limited quantitative comparison, undermining the significance of this claimed contribution.

The novelty of the core insight is somewhat limited: that adversarially trained models better maintain instruction-following and specification adherence under attack, and therefore benefit more from reasoning, is a relatively intuitive extension of known results on adversarial training and compositional/OOD generalization, with the 'RICH' largely restating this intuition in hypothesis form rather than providing fundamentally new theoretical insight.

Presentation issues: the paper's informal title and framing ('Get Rich or Die Scaling') together with the use of qualitative storytelling (snout counting, attention map interpretation) in place of more rigorous quantitative mechanistic analysis give the work a less rigorous feel than would be expected for a strong submission.

strengths: Addresses a concrete, well-motivated gap identified in prior work (Zaremba et al. 2025): why inference-compute defenses fail against gradient-based/multimodal attacks, and proposes a clear, testable hypothesis (RICH) to explain this.

Extensive and varied experimental protocol: black-box (Attack-Bard) and novel white-box PGD attacks, multiple perturbation budgets, multiple inference-scaling mechanisms (naive prompt repetition, CoT, budget-forced reasoning), and multiple model families (LLaVA-style, Qwen-2.5-VL-72B, Llama-3.2-Vision-90B, InternVL 3.5 gpt-oss 20B).

Thoughtful control experiments that help rule out confounds, e.g., pre-filling with random vs. clean tokens (Table 6), and random-token vs. specification-consistent scaling (Table 8), strengthening the causal story around instruction-following/compositional generalization rather than simply 'more tokens help'.

Practical, actionable takeaway: lightweight adversarial finetuning (e.g., FARE-style vision-encoder robustification) can unlock profitable inference-compute scaling, which is demonstrated concretely on InternVL 3.5 gpt-oss 20B (Figure 1, Appendix E).
Good qualitative supporting evidence (attention maps, reasoning traces, Claude-based description analysis in Appendix A) that adds interpretability to the quantitative claims.
Transparent limitations section acknowledging small-model scale and citing concurrent contrary evidence (Wu et al., 2025) on inverse scaling risks.
weaknesses: The central hypothesis, while clearly articulated, is somewhat expected/intuitive (robustified models generalize test-time instruction-following better to perturbed inputs); the 'compositional generalization' framing is asserted narratively but never directly measured or operationalized with a compositional-generalization-specific metric or test.

Several key experiments rely on very small sample sizes (e.g., Table 2/6 use 2 replicates; Table 3/7 use only 4 images × 3 attack variants = 12 per cell), which limits confidence in the robustness and generality of the quantitative trends, especially given the std/standard-error magnitudes reported.

The 'rich-get-richer' claim is largely based on raw PGD-step or loss differences; it is unclear whether this reflects a genuinely disproportionate (multiplicative/relative) benefit versus simply a ceiling/floor effect where more robust models have more room to show larger absolute gains as K increases. A normalized analysis controlling for baseline robustness level would strengthen this claim.

Results on larger-scale, non-robustified models (Qwen-2.5-VL-72B, Llama-3.2-Vision-90B, Table 5) show weak/inconsistent CoT benefits, which is consistent with RICH but also means the paper's main predictive power is demonstrated mostly on a narrow set of purpose-built, small LLaVA-style models with known robustness levels — the generality to frontier, RL-tuned reasoning models remains mostly unverified (only a single partially-robustified open model, InternVL, is tested with real reasoning scaling).

The claim of creating 'the first adversarially robust RL-tuned reasoning VLM' is somewhat overstated given the finetuning only robustifies the vision encoder with limited training (16K iterations, small batch size) and is evaluated on a narrow attack set.

The paper's writing is dense and notation-heavy (K, ε, multiple tables with overlapping settings across the main text and six appendices), which may hinder reproducibility and accessibility; some results (e.g., Figure 8's non-monotonic 'More ViT Adversarial Finetuning' curve) are not thoroughly explained.

No comparison to simple baselines combining adversarial training with fixed (non-scaled) inference compute to isolate exactly how much of the benefit is attributable to the interaction effect (synergy) claimed versus the additive effect of adversarial training alone.
